newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: STORMS CAUSE HAVOC IN SOUTHERN QUEENSLAND
In southern Queensland this morning, the clean up is underway after yesterday's wild storms which ripped up trees and brought down powerlines.
Some residents have decribed the gusty winds as mini-tornadoes.
In the Wide Bay region, storms tore through three districts, with the worst hitting the seaside village of Bargara near Bundaberg, where fourteen houses were damaged.
Further damage was caused to buildings at Poona near Maryborough and west of Biggenden where two more of the wild storms hit.
In the Taroom/Wandoan district late yesterday, storms uprooted trees and unroofed buildings.
CANBERRA CAR CRASH CLAIMS FOUR LIVES
Police believe a wet road contributed to an overnight accident which claimed the lives of a man and three children in Canberra.

A 40 year old man and three girls aged six, seven and eleven were killed after a van hit a street light on the Monaro Highway at Symonston last night and burst into flames. All four victims were from Canberra but their names have not been released.
GUN BUY-BACK BEGINS TODAY IN THE NT
In the Northern Territory, a national gun buyback scheme comes into effect today.
Owners of guns that will become prohibited under the Territory's gun control legislation can take them to a gun valuer, and have them valued for a twenty-dollar fee.
They'll then be able to take the gun and valuation to the police, when they'll be issued with a cheque to cover the gun and the valuation fee.
In Darwin and Alice Springs, the buy-back will occur on the spot, while in other centres, police will have to send the paperwork away.
PARACHUTING POLICY A FIRST FOR CAIRNS
In far north Queensland, the Cairns City Council is developing what's believed to be Australia's first local government policy on parachuting.
The Council has restricted the operations of the two local

parachuting groups in a bid to make them move their drop-zones out of the city's more built-up areas. Mayor, Tom Pyne, says his council's parachuting regulations will ensure that skydiving companies are fully aware of what conditions they have to meet when applying to establish a new landing point.
NORTH ARNHEM PEOPLE REJECT SPACE BASE
Aboriginal people from North East Arnhem land have rejected a proposal for a satellite launching facility near Darwin.
Consultants met with senior people of the Bawinanga Corporation to discuss the project that includes a fall out zone south-west of Maningrida.
If the facility goes ahead, 30 tonnes of space junk could fall as many as eight times a year, from a height of 50 kilometres.
The Corporation's David Bohn says everyone said no because the entire fall out zone is a cultural landscape.
MEMORIAL SERVICE TO BE HELD FOR CLIFF COLLAPSE VICTIMS
A memorial service will be on Thursday at Cowaramup Bay at
Gracetown in the south west of Western Australia for relatives and friends of the victims of Friday's rockfall which claimed 9 lives.
Five adults and four children died when a limestone cliff collapsed as they watched an end of term school surf carnival. Thursday's service is scheduled to begin at 11 o'clock.
Over the holiday long weekend in Western Australia, support has flowed in for relatives of victims and the only survivor, 10 year old Sarah Otto, who was dug out from under tonnes of sand and rock.
Her mother, Lyndell, died in the incident.
Messages of sympathy have come from the Prime Minister and Army chaplains at Townsville in Queensland, where 18 soldiers died earlier this year.
BIG SECURITY TO BE MAINTAINED IN BRYANT TRIAL
Police in Hobart say they want to ensure the security and safety of all concerned with the trial of the man accused of the Port Arthur shootings, whatever the cost.
Martin Bryant, aged 29, will stand trial in November after pleading not guilty to 72 charges, including 35 of murder in the Supreme Court yesterday.
Superintendent Ken O'Garey says around 70 officers were involved in yesterday's operation.
Superintendent O'Garey says a big police presence will be
maintained throughout the Bryant trial.
DOCTORS TO FIGHT ON AGAINST PROVIDER NUMBERS CHANGE
Junior doctors have vowed to fight on against continued Federal Government refusals to reconsider a planned cut to GP numbers.
Junior doctors and medical students are angry over the Government's decision to limit the number of Medicare provider numbers issued each year.
New doctors need a number to be able practice as GP's, and it's been claimed that up to 400 graduates will be left stranded by the move.
The Prime Minister says the cuts are quite defensible, and Health Minister Michael Wooldridge says he's yet to see a better alternative plan to reduce doctor numbers.
HOWARD PRAISES ITALIANS
Prime Minister John Howard has praised Italians for having having embraced mainstream Australia while still retaining a separate culture.
The Prime Minister praised the contribution Italians have made to Australia since the end of World War Two, in opening the Italo-Australian Welfare and Cultural Centre in Perth last night.
Mr Howard said the immense contribution Italians have made to the nation could be used as a model for multiculturalism.
Mr Howard is in Perth for a meeting of Federal Cabinet today.
"AIR RIGHTS" TO EXTEND OVER BROADCASTING?
Western Australia's Minister for Aboriginal Affairs, Kevin Prince, says there's little chance of native title being extended to include rights over broadcasting.
The State's Aboriginal Legal Service wants native title to include "air rights" to allow Aborigines to block English language radio and television broadcasts that undermine indigenous culture.
Executive officer, Dennis Eggington, says many Dreaming stories include accounts of ancestral beings travelling through airwaves, as they formed the landscape.
Mr Prince doubts the High Court would support proposals for such a claim, as it wasn't something that was inherent in the common law at the time of settlement.
ANZAAS CONFERENCE TO DISCUSS DEFENDING PLANET
Australia and New Zealand scientists have gathered in Canberra for the 65th ANZAAS conference to discuss issues on a theme of "Defending Our Planet."
A range of papers, from the the potential effects of an asteroid strike to genetic engineering in food production are on the agenda.
ANZAAS chairman, Professor Bruce McKellar says there is a negative perception of science in the general community that he hopes the conference can help change.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
